newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu touts pullback decision, Arafat critical.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu touts pullback decision, Arafat critical.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday his government's decision on a further West Bank troop withdrawal kept peace moves on track while not harming Israel's vital interests.
But both Palestinians and Netanyahu's right-wing coalition partners denounced the move.

The Palestinian self-rule Authority (PA) said Israel's decision to hand over nine percent of the West Bank -- including areas already under Palestinian civilian control -- was insufficient and its unilateral nature violated peace accords.
Israeli critics said Netanyahu gave too much. He emerged from a seven-hour overnight cabinet debate in fighting form after a 10-7 vote to backing his proposal.
Two percent of the land is exclusively under Israeli control; seven percent is land that had been patrolled by the Authority and Israel.
Israel already handed three percent of the West Bank to the PA since a 1993 peace deal, including eight major Arab towns.

"I think the important thing is that we gave an important chance for continuation of the peace process," Netanyahu told army radio. "We in fact handed over areas in which there is no (Jewish) settlement or security interest and on the permanent settlement map it is not vital to us."
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned the decision to reporters in Gaza: "This is a big deceit operation. It came from one party, without consultation with us."
Arafat aide Tayeb Abdel-Rahim told Israel Radio an official response would be decided later on Friday: "The latest decision is a violation of the agreement and we do not accept it."
He said the PA in a U.S.-brokered accord sealed in January on the three further Israeli West Bank withdrawals understood each would be 30 percent of the land now in Israeli hands.
Israel says the scope of the pullbacks are solely up to it.

Netanyahu's spokesman said the prime minister spoke both to U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and U.S. Ambassador Martin Indyk on Friday but gave no details. Netanyahu told Israel Radio he had not faced U.S. pressure.
Netanyahu, at a news conference later with German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, used Palestinian criticism to try to silence right-wing critics of the decision in his government.

"The Palestinian Authority said it is disappointed...It demands 30 percent of the area," he said. "That's what would have happened if there was a differenct government...These people (Israeli critics) who threaten have to ask themselves do they have a different government, do they have a better government."

The PA was already enraged at Israel's decision last month to build a new Jewish settlement of 6,500 homes in Arab East Jerusalem. About 3,000 Palestinians protested against the plans near the site on Friday under heavy Israeli security.
The U.S. State Department welcomed the new withdrawal as a "demonstration of Israel's commitment to the peace process," but added it hoped for more in the next stages of withdrawal.

The Israeli decision came hours before Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak left Cairo on his way to Washington, the latest Middle East leader to discuss the troubled peace process with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Israel said the pullback would take at least 48 hours. It must complete the third phase of redeployment by mid-1998. Final borders are to be decided in permanent status talks set to begin this month where Jerusalem is also to be negotiated.
Netanyahu earlier dismissed threats by eight members of his coalition to bolt over the pullback.

The government commands 66 of the 120 seats in parliament, although dissent has increased since the handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to the Authority in January. Netanyahu won Israel's May elections pledging to get tough with the PA.
